subject: Your account has been compromised
body: We noticed unusual activity on your account. Click here to secure it: https://paypa1-security.com/verify. Your account will be suspended in 1 hour if no action taken.

redFlags.explanation: The domain `paypa1-security.com` replaces the letter 'l' with the number '1' — a classic typosquatting trick.

redFlags.location: Your account will be suspended in 1 hour
redFlags.explanation: Legitimate companies rarely use 1-hour suspension threats. This is a pressure tactic common in phishing.
The URL directs to the typosquatted domain, not the real paypal.com.

explanation: This was phishing. Three red flags: typosquatted domain, urgency tactic, and a link to the fake site.

subject: Sign-in blocked
body: A sign-in attempt was blocked on your Google Account. If this was you, no action is needed. Your session remains active.
explanation: This email was safe. The sender domain matches Google exactly, there are no urgency tactics, and no suspicious links or attachments.

subject: Payment failed
body: We're having trouble charging your payment method. To avoid service interruption, update your billing info here: https://netf1ix.com/billing. Offer ends in 24 hours.

redFlags.explanation: The domain `netf1ix.com` replaces the letter 'i' with the number '1' — another typosquatting trick.
Creating false urgency to prompt quick, unthinking action is a hallmark of phishing.
The billing link points to the typosquatted domain, not the real netflix.com.

explanation: This was phishing. Two typosquatting indicators and an urgency tactic with a link to a fake domain.

subject: Unusual login detected
body: We detected a login from a new device on your checking account at 02:30 AM. If this wasn't you, secure your account immediately: https://bankofamerica.com/secure
explanation: This email was safe. The sender email matches Bank of America exactly. The link goes to the legitimate domain. No urgency tactics or suspicious attachments.

subject: Your Amazon Prime expired
body: Your Amazon Prime membership has expired. Renew now to keep your benefits: https://amazon-security.com/renew. Your membership will be cancelled permanently.

redFlags.explanation: The sender domain `amazon-security.com` is not the official Amazon domain. Legitimate Amazon emails come from amazon.com.
Threatening permanent loss of service is a pressure tactic used to manipulate victims into acting quickly.
The renewal link points to `amazon-security.com`, not the real amazon.com.

explanation: This was phishing. The sender domain is spoofed (not amazon.com), there's an urgency tactic, and the link leads to a non-Amazon domain.

subject: Your payslip is ready
body: Your monthly payslip for March is ready for download. Please find attached: payslip_march_2024.pdf

redFlags.explanation: An unsolicited attachment, especially a PDF, can contain malware. Legitimate payslips are typically accessed through an employee portal.

explanation: This was phishing. The unexpected PDF attachment is a red flag — legitimate companies typically don't send payslips as unsolicited attachments.

subject: Meeting invitation
body: You've been invited to a team meeting: "Q3 Review" on March 15 at 2 PM. Join via Teams: https://teams.microsoft.com/l/meetup-join/s/abc123def456
explanation: This email was safe. The sender matches Microsoft Teams exactly. The Teams link is legitimate. No urgency tactics, no suspicious attachments, and the domain is correct.

subject: Email quota exceeded
body: Your email storage has reached 95% capacity. To continue receiving messages, free up space immediately: https://company-update.com/quota. Your account will be disabled in 2 hours.

redFlags.explanation: The domain `company-update.com` looks plausible but is not the official company domain. Real IT notifications come from the corporate intranet.

redFlags.location: Your account will be disabled in 2 hours
redFlags.explanation: Similar to the 1-hour suspension claim, a 2-hour deadline creates false urgency to prompt quick action without proper verification.
The quota management link points to `company-update.com`, not the internal company system.

explanation: This was phishing. Typosquatting-ish domain, urgency tactic with account disable threat, and a link to a non-corporate domain.

subject: New connection request
body: Jane Doe wants to connect with you on LinkedIn. Accept the request or view her profile: https://linkedin.com/in/janedoe
explanation: This email was safe. The sender is linkedin.com (legitimate). The link goes to linkedin.com. No urgency tactics, no unexpected attachments. This is a normal LinkedIn notification.

subject: Tax refund pending
body: You are eligible for a tax refund of $842. Claim your refund before the deadline: https://irs-gov.net/refund. Act within 48 hours or the refund will be forfeited.

redFlags.explanation: The domain `irs-gov.net` uses `.net` instead of the official `.gov` — a common government impersonation trick.

redFlags.location: Act within 48 hours or the refund will be forfeited
redFlags.explanation: The IRS does not use 48-hour deadlines for refund claims. This pressure tactic is designed to make victims act before verifying.
The refund claim link points to `irs-gov.net`, not the real IRS government domain.

explanation: This was phishing. The domain uses .net instead of .gov, there's a 48-hour urgency tactic, and the link leads to a non-government domain.

subject: Unusual login from new location
body: We detected a login from an unfamiliar location. If this wasn't you, secure your account now: https://facebook.com/security-checkup
explanation: This email was safe. The sender is facebook.com (legitimate). The security checkup link goes to facebook.com. No urgency tactics beyond normal security notice, no suspicious attachments.

subject: Your subscription is cancelled
body: We were unable to process your payment. Your subscription has been cancelled. To reactivate, update your payment method: https://netflix.com/billing
explanation: This email was safe. The sender is netflix.com (legitimate). The billing link goes to the real netflix.com. This is a normal payment failure notification. No red flags.

subject: Your account is locked
body: Security measures have locked your checking account due to suspicious activity. To unlock your account, verify your identity: https://chase-security.net/verify. You have 24 hours to comply.

redFlags.explanation: The domain `chase-security.net` uses `.net` instead of the banking domain. Legitimate Chase communications use chase.com.
A 24-hour ultimatum to unlock your account is a pressure tactic. Banks typically use longer windows or phone verification.
The verification link points to `chase-security.net`, not the real chase.com.

explanation: This was phishing. The domain uses .net instead of .com, there's a 24-hour urgency tactic, and the link leads to a non-banking domain.

subject: Package delivery attempt failed
body: Your package at the UPS facility could not be delivered. Reschedule delivery: https://ups.com/reschedule
explanation: This email was safe. The sender is ups.com (legitimate). The reschedule link goes to the real UPS domain. This is a normal delivery notification. No red flags.

subject: Meeting recording available
body: A local recording of your Zoom meeting from March 14 is available. Download here: https://zoom-security.net/download. Files are deleted after 7 days.

redFlags.explanation: The sender domain `zoom-security.net` is not the official Zoom domain. Legitimate Zoom emails come from zoom.us.
Unsolicited download links for meeting recordings can deliver malware. Legitimate Zoom recordings are accessed through the Zoom web portal.
The download link points to `zoom-security.net`, not the real zoom.us domain.

explanation: This was phishing. The sender domain is spoofed (not zoom.us), there's an unexpected download link, and the link leads to a non-Zoom domain.

subject: Your password has been updated
body: Your PayPal password was successfully updated on March 17 at 08:15 AM. If you did not make this change, secure your account immediately: https://paypal.com/security-alert
explanation: This email was safe. The sender is paypal.com (legitimate). The security alert link goes to the real paypal.com. This is a legitimate password change notification. No red flags.
